item.title: 41. Show HN: BlastLoop, a structure-first coding method for AI agents
item.description:
14 points by rossleeshaw on 2026-10-15T16:26:39

BlastLoop is Ross Shaw's MIT-licensed coding framework for AI agents, organized around three writing altitudes—Blast for system-level structure and boundaries, Mid for subsystem-level work like feature slices and module refactors, and Inner for local, few-file changes—paired with a fixed three-stage test loop: T1 checks structure (routing corrections back to the right altitude), T2 fixes bugs and operational issues once structure is sound, and T3 adversarially attacks the result with edge cases, race conditions, security, and failure-path testing. If T3 finds a structural problem, the loop restarts at T1 and routes correction back through Blast, Mid, or Inner rather than patching locally. Positioning is explicit: it is not a fact-checker or truth engine, not a spec-then-plan workflow like GitHub Spec Kit, not a multi-agent org chart, and not red/blue testing alone—but a structure-first routing layer that can accommodate Spec Kit planning, vibe coding, focused prompts, or red/blue testing inside its altitudes and stages. Getting started takes under five minutes: clone the repo into the project, point the agent at AGENTS.md, load a build prompt matching the work's altitude, write code at that scope, then run T1 → T2 → T3 in order; docs/HANDOFFS.md covers the required handoff packet and routing rules, where test stages may recommend fixes but the owning altitude decides and implements them.

item.title: 42. How to be more ambitious: A tutorial for humans with models
item.description:
25 points by pretext on 2026-10-15T07:16:25

An Anthropic engineer working on Claude offers a tutorial on being more ambitious with AI tools, noting that model capabilities are uneven — "astounding in some directions, inadequate in others" (quoting Terence Tao) — and that many users barely scratch the surface. He defines ambition along four axes: Speed (same work, less time — the obvious economic value, so he skips it), Altitude (operate at a higher abstraction, focusing on the outcome beyond the task, such as shifting from "fix this crash" to "keep our apps crash-free," or asking Claude to design a better quarterly-review system than a deck — a mode that enables durable, human-out-of-the-loop workflows but works less well for creative work), Depth (push the model to use the raw data, tools, and statistical methods real field-leading experts would, set unreasonable-seeming goals, adversarially test business assumptions, generate new knowledge like early churn signals, and require outside validation rather than self-judging — he offers a prompt template asking what a top professional would do, what rawest material they'd use, what methods they'd apply, and what independent check would prove the result), and Range (draw on multiple disciplines, converting nouns into verbs to see what fields apply — e.g., a deck as "getting busy people to believe a story about cause and effect" — then assembling a "crew" of expert perspectives like analysts, journalists, short sellers, and forensic accountants to actually do research, not just role-play). All of this requires giving the model a computer with software-install ability and data access (e.g., MCP connectors). He concludes by arguing the advice is needed because humans are limited by narrow self-efficacy, citing research (Locke and Latham on specific hard goals), Patrick Collison's "Fast" list, Michelangelo's reluctance to paint the Sistine Chapel, Dantzig solving two "homework" problems that were actually unsolved, and Bannister's four-minute mile as evidence that believing in and witnessing the possible unlocks achievement.

item.title: 44. Making all divisions slower to fix a bug in 0.000000000000000000542% of cases
item.description:
34 points by marvinborner on 2026-10-15T00:56:13

Two's complement integer representation is asymmetric — the most negative signed value (e.g. -128 for 8-bit, INT_MIN for 32-bit) has no positive counterpart, so dividing it by -1 produces a value that cannot be represented. This matters for the Futhark compiler, which generates C code where signed integer overflow is undefined behaviour (and on x86 actually raises a CPU exception), making x/-1 with x equal to the most negative value both a spec violation and a potential crash. Since Futhark semantics define overflow as wrapping, the compiler represents all integers as unsigned C types to get well-defined overflow, but signed division must still use C's signed division operator, leaving this one dangerous case. The fix checks whether the divisor is -1 and, if so, performs the negation using unsigned arithmetic (e.g. `(int32_t)(0 - (uint32_t)x)`), which is defined and correct on target machines, at the cost of adding a branch to every signed division. Benchmarks show no measurable overhead on the Futhark GPU benchmark suite or on a sequential C backend (where the branch is easily predicted), but a deliberately division-bound program running on CUDA showed roughly a 2.3x slowdown (5548μs → 12592μs), because the branch interrupts instruction unrolling in the generated PTX; AMD GPUs showed a smaller but similar effect. The tradeoff is accepted as necessary for correctness, and the author notes this is the last known instance of undefined behaviour in Futhark's generated C code, though one instance of implementation-defined behaviour (oversized bit shifts) remains unfixed.

item.title: 45. An LSP layer for 70%+ token reduction in multi-turn agents
item.description:
3 points by productparker1 on 2026-10-15T20:20:55

The page presents UnlimitedAI™, a specification and compiled Rust CLI binary (`unlimited-bench`) for an in-container LSP daemon designed to cut token costs for AI coding agents like Claude Code, Cursor, Devin, and Replit. The tool intercepts stdio JSON-RPC streams, uses Tree-sitter AST parsing to prune non-cognitive syntax noise (imports, comments, docstrings), and routes only high-complexity work to cloud LLMs while handling syntax checks and structure locally. Claimed benchmarks from a simulated 25-step refactoring loop on a 150-file codebase include ~75% input token reduction (1.45M → 280k tokens), ~10.7x faster per-step latency (1,240ms → 115ms), and 80.6% cost savings ($21.75 → $4.20 per 1k runs). Token reduction varies by file type: ~15–30% for dense pure-function code and ~75–88% for production files with heavy imports and boilerplate. The enterprise architecture adds distributed AST state caching across agent fleets (sub-3.5ms retrieval of pre-pruned context), in-VPC edge execution, and zero-knowledge symbol masking (SHA-256) so unhashed source code never leaves the workspace, claimed as SOC2 compliant. The CLI runs against individual files with flags for distributed cluster simulation and optional queries; the full licensed product runs inside devbox containers with no host installation. The page concludes with an author bio describing an AI product strategy leader open to senior product roles, with contact at mgmtparker@gmail.com.

item.title: 46. Classify web pages before adding them to an AI agent's context
item.description:
4 points by ralphlaur on 2026-10-15T20:04:13

Sifty (sifty.dev) is an API that classifies a web page from its URL alone, before an agent or pipeline fetches it — returning a chosen label plus per-label probabilities without ever returning the page itself, keeping agent context clean and avoiding wasted reads on login walls, cookie notices, and 200-OK error pages. It can be pointed at a URL with custom labels or a free-text question, and supports use cases such as pre-filtering links before an agent opens them, ranking search results in parallel, asking multiple yes/no questions about one page at once (e.g., prices, free plan, enterprise plan), detecting quietly broken links that changed meaning while still returning 200, and triaging user-submitted links (product listing, spam, etc.). Pages cost 2 units each (3 with labels) regardless of how many questions are asked about them, with a free tier of 1,000 units per IP per day (~330 page checks); unreadable pages fail with a 502 while retaining their 2 units. Limitations: only public pages, links embedded in submitted text (up to 5 per request) are also read, long pages are sampled so distant facts can be missed, pages can misrepresent themselves, and accuracy has not been measured — the company advises verifying labels against known pages first. Sifty builds on syn, an open-source page-reading service available for self-hosting; API keys come from a verified account at sifty.dev/account.

The United Kingdom sanctioned cryptocurrency payment platform Cryptomus (formerly Certa Payments and Xeltox Enterprises, most recently renamed Heleket) on October 8, freezing its UK-held assets and barring British firms from doing business with it; VexPay, TokenSpot, and Tsunami Payments were also targeted. Cryptomus is described as a major payment hub for ransomware, narcotics, darknet markets, fraud, cybercrime services, child sexual abuse material vendors, terrorist financing, and human trafficking, helping Russia evade financial restrictions. Chainalysis reported the services received more illicit funds than all tracked mixers combined, with illicit counterparties exceeding 900 in a single month in late 2025, and TRM Labs found over $7 billion in transactions since 2022. After Canada levied a record CAD $176 million anti-money-laundering fine, Cryptomus appealed, launched Heleket as a parallel no-KYC service, and continued processing transactions; blockchain analyst Richard Sanders noted sanctions are more effective than fines since "a fine doesn't stop a cryptocurrency payment processor from processing payments." The move is the first known instance of a Five Eyes country sanctioning a crypto operation incorporated in another Five Eyes jurisdiction. Investigation found the entity's authority appears to stem from fake financial institutions overseen by a phony regulatory body in the disputed Western Sahara region: Cryptomus's sole shareholder was a 25-year-old Ukrainian woman who also headed WS Management and Advisory Corporation, which claims to license crypto, forex, and gaming businesses there via crasadr.com, and Cryptomus's former site shared a server with the website of the so-called Central Reserve Authority of Western Sahara.

item.title: 49. Company that put gas engines in Teslas goes bankrupt owing $37M
item.description:
11 points by Bender on 2026-10-15T23:15:39

Austrian engineering firm Obrist — long known for its "HyperHybrid" range-extender concept, including a modified Tesla Model 3 with a shrunken 17.3 kWh battery and a 40 kW two-cylinder generator in the frunk — is bankrupt. Three Obrist Group companies are insolvent with roughly €31.8 million in combined debts: Obrist Powertrain GmbH (€18.85 million, 34 creditors, nine employees), Obrist Technologies GmbH (€6.08 million, 10 creditors, no staff), and the German arm Obrist DE (€6.8 million). The Feldkirch Regional Court opened proceedings in late September after the firms filed petitions themselves, telling the court that neither continuing nor restructuring was possible; there is no rescue plan. The parent company, Obrist Engineering, which makes air-conditioning and thermal management parts with about 30 employees, is not part of the filings. Founder Frank Obrist blamed high development costs, failed investor talks, and Europe's auto industry crisis, while creditor group AKV also cited automakers' shift to fully electric vehicles. Despite over a decade of pitching, Obrist never put a production car on the road. It claimed in 2020 that an unnamed "international partner" had licensed the powertrain and that production cars would arrive by 2023 — neither happened. The pitch escalated over time: from a claimed €4,500 system cost, to a 2022 synthetic-methanol ("aFuel") Model Y prototype advertised as "climate-positive," to a 2024 announcement of a double-digit-billion-euro investment for methanol plants and "gigaplants" said to require some $50 trillion globally to replace fossil fuels. Obrist also lobbied Brussels to soften the EU's 2035 ban on new combustion cars, arguing its technology would emit 85% less CO2 than a battery-electric car. The commentary notes that range extenders themselves are viable — extended-range EVs sell strongly in China and are coming to North America — but characterizes Obrist as a licensing operation with no customer, whose claims kept outpacing results while battery prices fell and EV range improved. Its own bankruptcy filing citing the industry's move to full electrification underscores that its core bet failed.

item.title: 1. Things to know when you get cancer
item.description:

A patient diagnosed with squamous cell carcinoma of the mouth in May 2026 shares practical advice for navigating a cancer diagnosis: be aggressively persistent in scheduling appointments (call back repeatedly for cancellations), since delays can matter; be aware that AI chatbots may downplay symptoms and push toward "you don't have cancer"; push doctors to order comprehensive genetic testing promptly, as referral chains can cause multi-month delays; and take full ownership of your case with constant follow-ups. He recommends studying the NCCN "Standard of Care" guidelines (available as PDFs and an interactive navigator for non-professionals) to understand treatment options, using AI to help interpret them, talking to prior patients before consenting to surgery, asking surgeons about their annual procedure volume and complication rates, and getting a second opinion at a top cancer center as soon as the diagnosis is relatively clear—including a second pathology read. He suggests dictating notes after each appointment and having AI turn them into summary documents, checking out the Sijbrandij Foundation's resources and scheduling a call with them, and—if within a few hours' drive—being treated at a major cancer center (per U.S. News rankings) rather than a local community hospital, since top centers take most insurance and the biggest benefit is speed: at MD Anderson, a question could be answered in 20 minutes via a doctor's direct call to the pathologist, something his local oncologist would never have arranged.

item.title: 4. LFM2.5-24B-A2B: Built for fast on-device agents
item.description:

Liquid AI has released LFM2.5-24B-A2B, an open-weight reasoning model with 24B total parameters but only 2B active per token (top-4 routing across 64 experts, 40 layers), making it the largest entry in the LFM2.5 family and designed for fast, private on-device agents. Compared to its predecessor, it extends the context window from 32K to 131K tokens, doubles the vocabulary to 128K for better non-Latin tokenization, scales pretraining from 17T to 33T tokens, and adds large-scale reinforcement learning plus a five-stage post-training pipeline (SFT, teacher specialization, on-policy distillation, and agentic RL inside harnesses like OpenClaw and OpenCode); unlike LFM2-24B-A2B, it is reasoning-only, emitting an explicit chain of thought. It competes with larger MoEs such as Qwen3.6-35B-A3B (~50% more total and active parameters), leading or matching on five of eight agentic and tool-use benchmarks — including 48.09 vs. 38.19 on LiveClaw and 27.69 vs. 8.72 on AutomationBench — and all three instruction-following benchmarks, though larger models still win on knowledge-heavy (GPQA Diamond, HLE) and coding tasks (SWE-Bench Verified, SciCode); retrieval or web search is recommended to pair with its tool-calling strength. Thanks to the architecture it decodes at 184 tokens/s on an Apple M5 Max (114 tok/s on AMD Ryzen AI Max+ 395, up to 1.7× faster than comparable MoEs with the least memory) and exceeds 21K output tokens/s on a single NVIDIA B300 under SGLang, with day-one support for llama.cpp, MLX, vLLM, SGLang, and ONNX; the base and post-trained checkpoints are available on Hugging Face, with API pricing at $0.10/1M input ($0.05 cached) and $1.00/1M output.

item.title: 5. Americans' social activity has steeply declined in the past 30 years
item.description:
376 points by hubraumhugo on 2026-10-14T16:09:00

Data for Progress surveyed 1,098 U.S. adults in 2026 using questions replicating the DDB Needham Life Style surveys (1975–1999), which informed Robert Putnam's "Bowling Alone," and compared results with the 1995 survey. The findings show significant double-digit declines in Americans' participation in social activities over roughly three decades: attending a class or seminar (-22 points), entertaining guests at home (-21), attending church (-20), picnicking (-19), club meetings (-19), playing cards (-19), restaurant breakfast outings (-13), and volunteering (-12). Activities that saw increased engagement included internet use (+90), home video games (+22), exercise classes (+14), pop/rock concerts (+13), and personal airline travel (+5). The results fit within a broader picture of American social decline documented by other data, including the American Perspectives Survey finding that the share of Americans with five or more close friends fell from 63% to 38% between 1990 and 2021. The authors note a methodology caveat: because the two surveys used different sampling frames, modes, and weighting, the findings should be read as suggestive of trends rather than precise estimates of change.

item.title: 7. Better HTTP/1 connection reuse in Go 1.27
item.description:
245 points by allddd on 2026-10-14T16:29:33

Go 1.27's net/http.Transport automatically drains unread HTTP/1 response bodies (asynchronously, capped at 50 ms or 256 KB) before closing them, restoring connection reuse and making a benchmark of 100 GET requests against index.golang.org roughly 5x faster (~150 ms vs. ~710 ms on Go 1.26). The underlying issue: in HTTP/1.x, responses share a connection sequentially, so if a caller closes resp.Body without fully reading it, net/http through Go 1.26 must abandon the connection and repeatedly pay the TCP+TLS handshake cost (1–3 RTTs) for every subsequent request; HTTP/2 is unaffected since it multiplexes streams. This hidden cost can hit even code that only reads a status code or that stops just short of a body's end (e.g. encoding/json.Decoder leaving a trailing newline). The conventional manual fix—draining bodies with io.Copy, then bounding drain size with io.CopyN, bounding time with a timeout, and finally draining asynchronously to avoid blocking—proved error-prone and often misapplied (e.g. needlessly on HTTP/2). Go now handles this internally, skipping draining entirely when a `Connection: close` header makes it futile, so the recommendation is simply to close response bodies and let net/http manage the complexity.

TypeSafe is releasing Jev 1.14.0 along with experimental "danger zone" features aimed at developers who want to experiment rather than ship to production. These opt-in features, enabled via API headers, are intended to become permanent but are still too inconsistent to recommend for production use. TypeSafe also shares internal intelligence measurements — favoring only open-weight models due to validation-set and data-policy concerns — while cautioning users to trust their own evals, and notes that most future releases will be "beautifully boring": stability and deployment-focused improvements rather than flashy demos.

item.title: 12. How Amazon pushes up prices all across the Internet
item.description:
809 points by sighborg on 2026-10-14T09:28:17

The newsletter, marking Not-Ship's first anniversary, explains how Amazon's fee structure keeps consumer prices high — not just on Amazon, but across the entire retail market. Amazon takes roughly half of many sellers' sales through a stack of charges: a mandatory 15% referral fee plus optional but effectively compulsory fulfillment, storage, returns, and advertising costs, which the FTC calls "a virtual necessity for doing business on Amazon." Since sellers can't absorb these costs, they raise prices — and because the referral fee is a percentage, Amazon's cut grows as prices rise. Worse, Amazon's Fair Pricing Policy lets it remove the Buy Box or suspend sellers who offer products cheaper elsewhere, forcing sellers to keep prices high even on their own websites and at competitors like Target and Walmart; documented cases include sellers losing the Buy Box over Target sales and a suspension over a one-cent price gap. Since Amazon accounts for about 40% of US online retail, sellers can't realistically leave. The FTC and 17 states sued Amazon in 2023 over these practices, with trial expected next year, and Germany has ordered Amazon to stop controlling sellers' prices, though that decision isn't final. The piece closes with a disclosure about the author's past work at the Bezos-owned Washington Post, a nod to Cory Doctorow's "enshittification" concept, and links to related reading.

item.title: 14. Virtual Oxide Labs: Emulating a Full Oxide Rack
item.description:
116 points by tosh on 2026-10-14T18:21:14

sp-emu is an open-source tool that emulates the Cortex-M7 and Cortex-M33 service processors embedded in Oxide's racks, replacing the earlier SpSim stub with something that reproduces real behavior rather than just a happy path. It runs on illumos and Linux (x86 and ARM), with each device executing in a single thread and faithfully emulating the three core requirements: instructions, time, and interrupts. Hubris firmware can be flashed directly onto the emulated devices and reached over an ordinary socket, letting the Voxel lab communicate with them through the Management Gateway Service (MGS) and Inter-Processor Communication Channel (IPCC). The central difficulty is time. Since the firmware is written for silicon and Hubris schedules off a 1ms SysTick, while the emulator does not use wall time and emulated hardware is slower than the real thing, time is measured in instructions instead. A maybe_tick routine counts instructions against the kernel's own SysTick reload value and fires the exception wherever the single-priority design permits it — thread mode with interrupts unmasked. Peripheral accesses cost one instruction tick, versus dozens of bus cycles on real silicon. The exception_entry function models everything the hardware does when taking an exception, from "exception becomes active" to the first handler instruction, pushing the frame and reading the vector table via the bus. Because Hubris has a non-preemptible kernel that schedules tasks preemptively, SVCall, PendSV, SysTick and all IRQs share one priority level while faults take a higher one, so the emulator never needs to nest handlers. It checks pending IRQs against PRIMASK, FAULTMASK and BASEPRI, and if PendSV is pended it performs the deferred context switch. The whole thing boils down to a loop that steps one Thumb-2 instruction, advances the instruction-based SysTick, delivers interrupts, and every 4096 cycles pumps MGS packets and UART traffic over the host socket, running ad infinitum with everything else existing to make those calls feel real.

item.title: 15. Submarine cable resilience
item.description:
151 points by speckx on 2026-10-14T15:31:15

The world depends on roughly 1.5 million kilometres of submarine communications cables spanning some 607 systems, which satellite networks could not replace if they failed. These fibre-optic cables — about 20mm across in deep-sea sections, with armoured jacketing only near shore — are remarkably reliable themselves, but around 200 faults are reported yearly, driven mainly by maritime activity: about 86% stem from fishing or anchoring, with geological events, abrasion and component failure accounting for the rest, and nearly half of faults occurring in territorial waters where cables are most exposed. Vulnerable choke points include the Bab al-Mandab Strait (16 cables, severed in September 2025, cutting 25% of Asia-Europe-Middle East capacity), the Singapore Strait (35 systems) and the Luzon Strait (18 cables), where a 2006 earthquake and landslips took 11 repair ships 49 days to fix. Deliberate sabotage has a long history, from British cuttings of German cables in 1914 and 1939 to repeated outages between Taiwan and the Matsu Islands — 27 cuts between 2018 and 2022 plus four major outages from 2023 to 2025 — and 11 Baltic Sea disruptions since 2023. Resilience relies on careful cable routing (short, deep, geologically stable, away from politically unstable waters and choke points), cable protection zones, secure landing stations, and, when faults occur, optical reflectometry to locate breaks and specialist repair vessels that grapnel, splice and re-lay the cable — a job costing typically USD 500k–1M that requires government permission, since under UNCLOS sovereign authority extends 12 nautical miles offshore and resource rights to 200, making permitting delays an increasing obstacle to repairs.

item.title: 17. Passkeys are not a trap
item.description:
588 points by speckx on 2026-10-14T15:15:45

A widely shared post claiming passkeys are a "trap" because they enable website attestation — supposedly leading to logins restricted to approved software and operating systems — is rebutted point by point by the author, who has extensive hands-on experience building passkeys libraries and tools. Synced passkeys stored in iCloud Keychain, Google Password Manager, 1Password or Bitwarden return no attestation statement at all, so a consumer site demanding attestation would instantly lock out nearly all its users; industry guidance has long told consumer sites not to request it. Attestation, when present, only reveals the authenticator's make and model via its AAGUID and a vendor certificate chain — it discloses nothing about your OS, browser, extensions, root/jailbreak status, or firmware. The original post's recommendation to use a hardware key like a YubiKey is especially confused, since YubiKeys ship with Yubico attestation certificates and enterprise attestation exists precisely to mandate approved hardware. Replacing passkeys with TOTP is also a downgrade: TOTP codes can be phished via relay kits like Evilginx, whereas passkeys are cryptographically bound to the domain, so they can't be used on lookalike sites and leave nothing for the user to get wrong. The author's advice is to keep using passkeys wherever offered, store them in a manager you trust and that supports portability, and push back loudly if attestation ever does creep into consumer logins — but avoiding passkeys today only leaves you more exposed to phishing.

item.title: 20. Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
item.description:
201 points by jascha_eng on 2026-10-14T11:47:53

pg_vectorsearch (PRISM) is an alpha-stage PostgreSQL extension providing a high-performance approximate nearest neighbor index access method, implemented in C and released under the PostgreSQL License. Its PRISM index (Partitioned Routing Index for Similarity Matching) targets 100M+ vector workloads and is conceptually similar to pgvector's IVFFlat, but combines a hierarchical centroid tree for partitioning, RaBitQ quantization with theoretical error bounds for a two-stage estimate-and-rerank search, a SIMD-optimized page layout for distance computation (AVX2, AVX512, NEON), and reliance on PostgreSQL's buffer cache and async I/O. The project claims significant speedups over pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW for both queries and index builds, including faster performance at equivalent recall than HNSW on a 100-million-vector dataset with a quarter of the memory. It supports dynamic inserts, updates and deletes, with oversized posting lists split via the prism_rebalance procedure. Users can either store vectors in the extension's own vec32/vec16 columns (no other extension needed) or install it alongside pgvector and index existing vector/halfvec columns unchanged; both paths use the same operators (<->, <#>, <=>) and tuning knobs, with L2, inner product, and cosine operator classes available and prism.nprobe as the main adjustment. Prerequisites are PostgreSQL 18+, a C11 compiler (GCC 11+/Clang 14+), and the Meson build system, with CBLAS optional; docs cover tuning, maintenance, architecture, SIMD, development, and related research (RaBitQ, SPFresh, SPANN, ScaNN, pgvector, pgvectorscale).

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing.- pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW index has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that).- pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out.- pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.

I've written a short technical deep dive into the architecture of its PRISM index to answer some, thought I'd share:https://www.linkedin.com/pulse/inside-pgvectorsearch-archite...

item.title: 22. Show HN: I wrote an email app that accepts only one sender per inbox
item.description:
100 points by edpin2000 on 2026-10-14T17:00:59

Clova.Email is a privacy-focused email aliasing service that generates unlimited disposable inboxes so you never share your real address. It offers three inbox types: one-sender inboxes, which are permanently claimed by the first sender to write in — bouncing everyone else, so a leaked or resold list becomes worthless; temporary inboxes with a set lifetime (an hour for a download link, a month for a trial) that stop accepting mail and can wipe their contents when they expire; and prefix inboxes, where you claim a five-character-or-more prefix and then use any suffix you like instantly, with each address still locking to its first sender. Three plans are available: Free ($0) with unlimited inboxes, one permanent address, one prefix, one forwarding address and 100 MB storage; Pro ($30/year) with 5 permanent addresses, 25 prefixes, 10 forwarding addresses and 10 GB; and Business ($50/year), which adds bring-your-own-domain, any address at that domain, unlimited permanents and forwarding, and 25 GB. Message limits are 100 per day on Free and 1,000 on Pro and Business. The service also supports MCP, letting AI assistants like Claude or Cursor create inboxes and retrieve incoming codes and messages under permissions you control. The company states it doesn't sell user data, read mail, track users, or use sign-in data for advertising; full data export is available on any plan, and sign-in works via Google, passkey, or username and password.

item.title: 23. Iosevka is an open-source, sans-serif and slab-serif monospace font
item.description:
716 points by otobrglez on 2026-10-14T08:27:59

William Dwight Whitney's principle — that prehistoric language change must be explained only by factors observable in the historical period — underpins a reassessment of a classic problem in Indo-European philology: why the ancestor of the Indo-European languages assigned grammatical gender, distinguishing masculine, feminine, and neuter. The puzzle is familiar to anyone who has studied Greek, Latin, French, or German, where inanimate objects are arbitrarily marked as male or female (*der Fuß* but *die Hand*; *hīc hortus* but *haec planta*; ὁ πλοῦτος but ἡ πενία). Because the gender system pervades all the older Indo-European languages, it must date to the pro-ethnic Indo-European community itself. The author presents this problem as an illustration of how modern theories of language development differ in method from those held by the founders of comparative philology in the early and mid-nineteenth century — a methodological shift shared with neighboring fields of philological and historical research.

item.title: 25. Yandex outage: data shows that instead of going dark, malicious bots moved
item.description:
255 points by coloneltcb on 2026-10-14T20:29:13

Claims that Ukrainian drone strikes on Yandex data centers knocked Russian bot farms offline are not supported by Cloudflare's network data. Between October 7–13, traffic to Yandex's two autonomous systems collapsed — 99% below baseline for Yandex Search (AS13238) and 90% for Yandex.Cloud (AS200350), settling around 85–90% down — but the traffic that vanished differed sharply: the Search ASN's requests were 99.5% automated yet 93.6% verified, dominated by YandexBot, YandexRenderResourcesBot, and YandexImages crawling pages, images, and news articles, so the main effect was reduced search indexing. Yandex.Cloud's bots were unverified, application-like traffic; while WordPress plugin probing fell 90% and scanner requests 93%, high-volume automation simply migrated to other Russian hosting providers such as Radist and Selectel, with identical JA4 TLS fingerprints, headers, paths, and User-Agents — gambling-sector bot traffic targeting one account dropped to zero on Yandex.Cloud while total Russian gambling bot requests stayed essentially flat, rising 1.4%. Globally, bot traffic as a share of HTTP requests was unchanged (~39.4%), Russia-origin bot traffic fell only proportionally, and social media post/reply/like endpoint traffic showed no unusual shift, offering no evidence that influence operations were crippled. The analysis concludes that aggregate ASN traffic volume is an unreliable indicator of malicious activity, since cloud workloads are portable and defenders should instead inspect request behavior, fingerprints, and WAF responses.

item.title: 26. America didn't lose its rare earth industry, it sold it
item.description:
175 points by speckx on 2026-10-14T17:50:26

China's October 2025 rare earth export controls have been extended only through short, concession-securing reprieves (currently to Nov. 10, within a broader truce to Jan. 10, 2027), and Beijing even added U.S. hopefuls MP Materials and USA Rare Earth to its control list in June—evidence of real leverage over a market worth under $10 billion that underpins trillions in global output. China refines over 90% of the world's rare earths and nearly 99% of heavy rare earths, a chokepoint built deliberately since Deng Xiaoping's 1964 orders and cemented when U.S. firms rationally exited a dirty, low-margin business (e.g., Mountain Pass's closure, GM's 1995 sale of Magnequench), treating rare earths as a market when Beijing treated them as strategy. That mismatch creates a classic market failure: no private capacity is built while China floods the market, and none can be stood up quickly when supply is cut, as Japan discovered in 2010. Although up to $100 billion in One Big Beautiful Bill Act loan authority exists, existing deals like the July 2025 MP Materials package blur two roles—ordinary lending and geopolitical insurance—leaving them exposed to budget cycles and political turnover. The authors propose a contingent convertible (CoCo) security paired with a guaranteed offtake price floor: it starts as a simple interest-paying loan, converts to a share of the producer's free cash flow once a capacity threshold is met, and additionally converts to common equity if Beijing's behavior—objectively measured supply denial or a price-band breach, not Beijing's own admission—triggers a cutoff. Producers gain a put-like price floor to survive Beijing's dumping while surrendering upside (a call), and taxpayers are paid for the risk actually borne rather than for risk that never materializes.

item.title: 27. Nvidia's first GPU: GeForce 256
item.description:
74 points by ibobev on 2026-10-14T12:05:44

Nvidia released the GeForce 256 on October 11, 1999, calling it the first GPU, though the designation is somewhat arbitrary since competitors like 3dfx were offloading graphics work from the CPU years earlier (and Commodore did so with the Amiga in 1985) — Nvidia simply coined the term. The card wasn't an immediate game changer, performing well for budget systems with low-end CPUs like 300 MHz Celerons, but faster CPUs could outperform its hardware transform and lighting. The post also recounts Nvidia's near-collapse: in 1996, three years after its 1993 founding, Nvidia failed to complete a Sega Dreamcast graphics chip contract, and Sega bailed the company out with a $5 million investment (later earning a $10 million profit). That funding allowed Nvidia to develop the Riva 128, the successful TNT2, and ultimately the GeForce 256. Without Sega's money, Nvidia might have gone bankrupt before 3dfx did; instead, Nvidia bought most of 3dfx's intellectual property in December 2000, and 3dfx declared bankruptcy in October 2002.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. Per The NVIDIA Way [1], the GeForce 256 was branded as "the first GPU" for marketing reasons alone; the actual first GPU was the subsequent GeForce 3 (which introduced programmable shaders): [Sanford] Russell grabbed Michael Hara for a thirty-minute brainstorm session to figure out how to market the GeForce 256 more effectively, and both executives remember coming out of the room with the notion to call the new chip the first entry in an entirely new product category altogether: a graphics processing unit, or GPU, which would be to graphics rendering what the computer's main central processing unit (CPU) was for all other computational tasks. Even so, the GPU moniker, when applied first to the GeForce 256, was controversial among Nvidia engineers, who pointed out that a chip could not truly be called a GPU unless it had several features that the GeForce 256 did not. The chip lacked a "state machine," a technical term meaning a dedicated processor that transitions from various states to execute and fetch instructions, in the same manner that a CPU does for programming commands. It was not programmable, meaning that graphics styles and features could not easily be customized by third-party developers. Instead, developers would have to rely on a fixed set of Nvidia-defined hardware functions. Moreover, the GeForce 256 did not have its own programming language. But the marketing team argued that such features were already planned for the next generation of graphics chips. And even without them, the GeForce 256 delivered a step change in performance that would be obvious to every gamer and computer enthusiast in the world. While not literally a GPU, the GeForce 256 could still be a category-defining product. The chips that would follow-the "true" GPUs that would be fully programmable by outside developers-were coming soon enough. So Nvidia's marketing team pushed forward with the GPU name over the dissent of Nvidia's engineers. "We don't need anyone's approval," Vivoli told them. He didn't think anyone outside of the industry would really care about the technical definition. Besides, "we knew the next one was going to be programmable. We decided to take a leap, make a stretch that this is a GPU." In February 2001, Nvidia released the GeForce 3, whose programmable shader technology and support for third-party development of its core graphics functions made it the first true GPU. [1] https://www.taekim.com

item.title: 29. Smart people don't think others are stupid (2012)
item.description:

The post argues that intelligence is a behavior, not a type of person: there are no inherently smart or stupid people, only moments of being smart or stupid. Being smart means thinking things through and genuinely searching for the real answer, while being stupid means avoiding thought by jumping to an easy conclusion — effectively quitting the question and losing by default. Saying "I don't know" is therefore usually the smart move, since it refuses to leap to a conclusion. Labeling others as stupid (whether Southerners, liberals, or any other group) reveals that the speaker has stopped thinking, because doing so is satisfying and shortcuts the effort of reasoning. The conclusion: truly smart people don't think other people are stupid.

item.title: 30. Running Windows desktop tests from Linux with disposable VMs
item.description:
89 points by jadenlemmon on 2026-10-14T14:55:19

QA Wolf built infrastructure for testing Windows desktop apps at scale by treating Windows VMs like mobile devices rather than servers: each test claims a disposable, single-use VM from a warm pool on Google Compute Engine, uses it once, and destroys it, with a fresh machine taking its place. Because Windows UI Automation requires a logged-in graphical session and cold VMs take 2–3 minutes to boot, a Kubernetes-based device scheduler (extending the same service that hands out Android emulators) maintains pools of already-booted, logged-in VMs via custom resources (WindowsVMTemplate, WindowsVMPool, WindowsVM), tracks fleet state durably, reclaims machines whose tests go silent for 60 seconds, spills capacity to other zones, and rolls out new machine images by attrition rather than patching. Test code stays in a Linux runner pod and connects to each VM over three channels—Playwright via CDP for browsers, WebdriverIO/Appium/WinAppDriver for native apps, and a WebRTC screen stream for live viewing and recording—exposed through a single unified `@qawolf/flows/windows` API (`launch()` and `startApp()` with shared expect matchers). Custom base images baked by PowerShell script pre-install automation tooling, run a separate root session, and pre-clear first-run dialogs; customer-supplied scripts can produce private images for licensed or specialized software. Apps reach each new VM without touching the runner, via short-lived signed URLs downloadable only over Google's internal network, with support for .exe, .msi, and .ix installers.

item.title: 31. Gaming on Linux without cheating
item.description:
75 points by water-drummer on 2026-10-14T14:19:02

Epic's Easy Anti-Cheat is addressing Linux anti-cheat parity with Windows through two tracks. The long-term ideal is an operating-system-level guarantee that player data stays isolated from both anticheat and game companies while preventing gameplay tampering — virtualization-based approaches have tried this but haven't gained traction, and Epic says it will keep working with willing industry partners, including maintaining an open line with Valve to support Steam Hardware devices to the maximum extent technically possible. For the near term, Epic is rebuilding its Linux anti-cheat as EAC Linux v2, using existing Linux features — signed kernel, signed kernel modules, and secure boot with attestation — to bring protection much closer to Windows levels. These requirements build on work Linux distribution maintainers already do, so the more distributions meet them by default, the fewer players will need to reconfigure to play. Epic is engaging Linux community leaders and will co-host a panel later this year with Fedora Project Leader Jef Spaleta on enabling fair competitive gaming on Linux. EAC Linux v2 will be piloted first in Fortnite to test and refine it in a live environment, after which it will be made available to other developers so they can bring multiplayer games to Linux.

The fairness (compliance) goal demands that this software runs correctly and only conveys information and processes input as designed. The user control (freedom) goal demands that the individual user is allowed to run and modify any software as they see fit, including any game software, meaning that he or she must be able to tamper with the game software behaviour to gain advantage.Now remember that online gaming is an extremely low-trust environment. item.title: 32. Show HN: Graphicle, a Rust port of Graphify with memory for coding agents
item.description:
45 points by KarLexAI on 2026-10-14T15:00:41

Graphicle is a free, Apache-2.0-licensed tool (by KarLex AI) that gives coding agents a code graph and persistent project memory in a single native Rust program that runs locally — no account, API key, or telemetry required. It parses your repository with tree-sitter into a graph of files, functions, classes, calls and imports, and indexes docs (Markdown, PDF, Office, HTML), reviewed decisions, and past Claude Code/Codex sessions into a searchable memory store, all held in one SQLite file. `graphicle setup` indexes the repo and auto-connects found agents (Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, VS Code, Claude Desktop, any MCP client) via a single MCP server exposing Graphify-compatible tools like `query_graph` and `shortest_path`; everything it changes is backed up and reversible with `graphicle disconnect`. Agents get cited excerpts (file and line) within a token budget without Graphicle calling a model itself — a model is only needed for `graphicle ask` answers, agent-proposed memories (which require user approval), and full document extraction. It features session capture, Git-hook syncing, stale-memory detection tied to code changes, cross-repo workspace recall, impact analysis (`graphicle graph affected`), an interactive browser app (`graphicle open`), and hash-chained deletion receipts. Benchmarks claim it outperforms Graphify in extraction speed (3m18s vs 26m38s on a 31k-file Kubernetes repo) and competes well against seven memory systems; native Windows support is planned, and a commercial team edition is in private preview.

item.title: 33. Scientists are teaching birds to sing lost songs
item.description:
49 points by speckx on 2026-10-14T13:20:44

Birdsong is increasingly recognized as a conservation issue: as populations decline, fewer fledglings learn the complex, dialect-specific songs they need to attract mates, defend territory, and breed successfully. Physicist Gabriel Mindlin's team at the University of Buenos Aires tested whether lost songs could be restored by playing computer-generated renditions of a rufous-collared sparrow tune that had vanished from a Buenos Aires park since the 1960s, based on hand-drawn annotations; within three months a local bird began imitating parts of it, though only a few individuals still sing it. Broader research shows that songbirds (about 4,000 of the world's 10,000 bird species) share common song "motifs" shaped by their environments, and that translocated or captive-bred birds often produce abnormally poor songs — as with cirl buntings moved from Devon to Cornwall, whose songs recovered within eight years, partly after playback. Australian regent honeyeaters learned proper songs from just two wild-born male tutors, though live tutoring risks distress and disease, prompting interest in AI-based tutoring. Experts note dialect mismatches hinder pairing and survival, and stress the value of systematically recording and archiving birdsong as populations change.

item.title: 36. Neckbeard – A DevOps/platform/SRE plugin for your agent
item.description:
67 points by bealesh on 2026-10-14T17:45:34

Neckbeard is an open-source (Apache-2.0) plugin for coding agents — Claude Code, Codex, Cursor, or anything reading a SKILL.md — that converts an app into reviewable cloud infrastructure with cost estimates attached. It addresses the problem that agents generate plausible but unvetted IAC with no sense of security exposure or price. The workflow splits responsibilities: the agent reads your repo (Dockerfiles, ports, env vars, Procfiles), produces an evidence-backed app profile with file/line citations and confidence levels, asks questions code can't answer (traffic, tolerable downtime, whether Postgres is new or existing), and then maps answers onto a human-maintained catalog of versioned, CI-tested OpenTofu modules scoped to specific workload shapes; the middle is deterministic Go that emits a hash-verified blueprint.yaml and refuses to overwrite user-edited files. Commands include /neckbeard:analyze, :estimate (Infracost-powered monthly cost table with unpriced resources named and low/expected/high scenarios), :sync (scaffold, validate), :doctor, and :help. It covers AWS, GCP, and Azure with GitHub Actions or GitLab CI, as serverless containers (Cloud Run, ECS Fargate, Container Apps) or Kubernetes (EKS, GKE, AKS), with OIDC-only auth, private networks, and Trivy/HIGH-CRITICAL blocking. A sample reference app costs $77/mo on Cloud Run up to ~$801 on AKS, illustrating that Kubernetes isn't yet sensible for solo developers. Validation is honestly tiered as V0 (static syntax/policy), V1 (authenticated plan) and V2 (verified deployment), with the latter two marked NOT EXERCISED until a human runs them. It's pre-alpha: the analyze/plan/estimate/scaffold/validate path is CI-tested across all 12 cloud × VCS × runtime combinations, and live serverless-container deploys have worked on AWS/GitHub and Azure/GitHub, while GCP, GitLab lanes, Kubernetes, and landing zones remain implemented but unexercised.

item.title: 37. Strands Decider: Why Not an Encoder?
item.description:
37 points by surprisetalk on 2026-10-14T14:40:03

The author investigates why strands-decider-2B, a fine-tuned decoder LLM used for entailment/verification judgments, was built as a causal model rather than a bidirectional encoder, by comparing five designs: v19 (the shipped Qwen3.5-based 2B decoder with Gated DeltaNet layers), two T5Gemma 2 encoder-decoder variants (1B+1B and 4B+4B), and two encoder-only models (a plain 2.6B T5Gemma encoder, and a latency-optimized variant with a masked state cache that allows parallel question evaluation). Results show the large 8B encoder-decoder beat v19 on JevBench accuracy and Brier calibration, but at 4× the parameters; the ~2.6B masked encoder (e1b) roughly matched v19 on accuracy and calibration while cutting median latency from ~65ms to ~35ms. However, the encoder scales worse with prompt length because all its attention layers are quadratic, whereas 75% of v19's layers use linear-cost Gated DeltaNet, giving v19 a higher latency floor but better asymptotic behavior—so e1b's advantage depends on having mostly short prompts. The unmasked encoder (e1a) beat v19 on seven of nine individual tasks but scored notably worse on JevBench and somewhat worse on JF100, hinting that allowing the state to attend to the question during reading may hurt generalization. The author concludes no clear winner emerges, since the experiment confounds architecture, base models, and tuning differences, and the code remains in a side branch rather than being merged into mainline strands-decider.

item.title: 40. What agents mean for Rust (and vice versa)
item.description:
69 points by mfrw on 2026-10-14T08:49:06

A Rust programming language designer reflects on whether LLMs and agentic coding make language design skills obsolete, concluding they do not: humans still have a role in programming, and Rust in particular is a strong fit for agentic development (citing rapid growth, e.g., Meta writing more first-party Rust this year than the previous nine combined). The post frames an effective "software factory" as resting on three pillars — design, construction, and optimization — and argues Rust does well on the latter two. On optimization, Rust's good-performance-by-default design plus its low-level knobs (allocation control, struct layout, boxing, inline assembly) pair well with agents, which prove adept at fine-tuning existing code, from hand-tuned cryptographic assembly to diagnosing async pitfalls with profilers; the goal is to keep the "low-level enough for a kernel, high-level enough for a GUI" balance, tolerating a bit more explicit clone()/share() noise. On reliability, Rust's type system keeps agents "on track" with an "if it compiles, it works" feel, since tests alone can't show correctness — agents often miss the intended logic entirely. But types only rule out certain wrong things, not prove correct behavior, so proof tools like Verus, Creusot, Aeneas, and Kani matter; notably, proofs enable more aggressive optimization (proving unsafe code is actually safe), and Rust's borrow checker simplifies proof obligations enough to make tools like Verus fast and reliable. The author recommends Rust double down on "if it compiles, it works" by extending what its type system can express, making the compiler extensible so proof tools are no longer a janky, macro-heavy, pinned-version experience, and proposes a north star of "no more unsafe code" — not banning the unsafe keyword, but gaining the ability to prove all unsafe code cannot cause undefined behavior, helping stem the flow of CVEs given agents' ability to find vulnerabilities. The post was written as a companion to a REBASE/SPLASH talk, and touches on related research including Reachability Types, Information Borrowing, Hylo's projections, and the Rue language work, before turning to design as the remaining open problem (the text cuts off there).

item.title: 43. A new model for open source: closed to pull requests, open to remix
item.description:
14 points by ghuntley on 2026-10-14T23:40:28

The author proposes a post-GitHub, post-AI open source development model called the "Remix Model," arguing that neither Raymond's "cathedral" (small exclusive teams, polished infrequent releases) nor the "bazaar" (decentralized pull-request workflow as embodied by GitHub) is adequate now. Even before AI, the bazaar model bred entitlement—users nagging maintainers to merge changes and expecting unpaid maintenance—and AI-generated pull requests have made review pointless; what matters is the idea, not the patch. Since open source licenses already permit remixing, and the old barrier was merely a knowledge gap that AI agents have eliminated, the Remix Model works as follows: publish source and intent under an as-is license; others express desired changes as small Nix overlays (defined once and reused across devenv shells, Docker images, NixOS systems, tests, CI, and agent sandboxes) instead of forking or submitting pull requests; the valuable unit becomes the idea rather than the patch; maintainers may adopt, reimplement, or ignore contributions with no obligation to review or maintain; and useful adaptations surface as a proliferation of overlays that others can discover, compose, and even feed back upstream via agents. Concretely, the author says he will disable pull requests on his GitHub projects, keep discussions open, and publish remixing guidance—illustrated by a demo where a consumer disables Git force-push via a single overlay applied consistently across environments, rather than filing an upstream PR. He believes reducing the cognitive burden of maintaining open source will lead to far more software being released.

Design Creativity Bench is a new benchmark measuring how creative frontier AI models are at UI design, evaluated across 16 leading models on 80 open-ended UI tasks, each rendered in two product domains with human designer references as a baseline. Unlike existing UI benchmarks that track a single output-quality metric, it assesses three dimensions: originality (how distinct a model's designs are from other models' outputs for the same brief), creative range (how much design decisions shift when the domain changes), and appropriateness (how well the UI meets the brief's functional requirements). Results show a substantial creativity gap — the top model, OpenAI's GPT-6 Astra, scores 65.5 versus a human reference of 92.3 — suggesting that even as models grow better at generating functional websites and product UIs, they still struggle with creative design decisions. The full leaderboard, methodology, reproducible evaluation framework, paper, HuggingFace dataset, and GitHub repository have been published.

item.title: 45. Is 'Attention' the Essence of Intelligence?
item.description:
82 points by bcaulfield on 2026-10-14T03:10:25

The modern AI boom traces back to a 2014 University of Montreal project in which intern Dzmitry Bahdanau, with adviser Yoshua Bengio and postdoc Kyunghyun Cho, tackled English-to-French machine translation with neural networks. Their fix for the bottleneck that made long sentences translate poorly was an operation they called "attention," which lets a network focus on the most relevant words anywhere in a source sentence when producing each output word — for instance, deciding whether "it" in "The animal didn't cross the street because it was too tired" refers to the animal (masculine *il*) or the street (feminine *elle*). In 2017 Google's "Attention Is All You Need" paper built the transformer architecture around attention alone, achieving state-of-the-art results at a fraction of the compute and spawning ChatGPT, Claude, and the broader LLM era. The mechanism works by converting each word into a vector and generating query, key, and value vectors; parallel attention heads match queries against keys to weight how much each word's value updates a word's representation, so context is encoded into math and refined across layers, with an encoder building understanding and a decoder emitting translations. Nothing about semantics is hand-coded — associations such as animals getting tired emerge from trillions of error-correction adjustments during training on paired text. Because predicting the next word in a translation is a special case of predicting the next word generally, training on the whole internet to do that reportedly forces models to master translation, arithmetic, facts, and mathematics; co-author Llion Jones calls this "AI-complete," suggesting next-word prediction may be the closest available operational definition of intelligence, though he cautions the current paradigm likely won't solve efficiency and requires something very different going forward.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. As an NLP person it's very hard for me to endorse this explanation, because the Vaswani et al transformer (as it is described here) simply does not work until you add the most important ingredient of all: the positional encoding.Most of the semantics of a sentence are indicated by the precise order the tokens appear. This is easiest to see in a language like English, since it is visible in two very prominent ways.First, the morphology is fairly derivational, meaning you can keep adding suffixes to things and English speakers will generally get what you mean. For example, add some more suffixes to that word: derivational-ish-ly. You've probably never heard this specific variant, but you still probably have some idea of what it means anyway. The transformer can only capture these semantics if it has some representation of the fact that the suffixes inflect the meaning of the word's root (presumably something like `deriv`). English encodes this entirely by the position of the suffixes relative to the root. Without the positional information, there is no way to recover it, and sentences would lose much of their meaning, since English depends heavily on this construction.Second, English has relatively few cases, and thus relies very heavily on the order of words to indicate what is the subject and what is the object. English specifically is Subject-Verb-Object, and the instinct of native English speakers to use SVO ordering is so strong, you will find them inserting nouns and pronouns into sentences that do not actually have subjects at all. "It's raining outside" is the most famous example. This sentence has no subject at all, and yet native English speakers feel a strong need to place "it's" at the beginning.If the transformer did not have positional encodings it would be completely hopeless to recover what is the subject and what is the object from English sentences. There simply is no other way to reliably tell, other than inspecting the word positions.It's worth noting we also do have the counterfactual. Generative language models that explicitly exclude positional information, like Latent Dirichlet Allocation, are only able to (essentially) cluster word co-occurrences. That is not as useless as it sounds—if I say "fire house burning ambulence" you kind of get the point even without a subject or an object—but it certainly does not generate the lucid, provoking sentences that modern LLMs do.
  2. This is the core insight, some in the original grad student author's own words:https://www.quantamagazine.org/is-attention-the-essence-of-i..."Sentences with pronouns such as “it” in them illustrate the challenge that attention overcomes. Consider: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too tired.” And: “The animal didn’t cross the street because it was too wide.” To translate these sentences correctly into French, an AI model must determine that, in the first one, “it” refers to the animal, which is a masculine word in French, so the translation should use that form of the pronoun, il. But in the second sentence, “it” refers to the street, a feminine word that requires a different pronoun, elle. How can the machine figure this out?""Bahdanau remembered doing translation exercises when he was learning English in school. To write each next word of his translated sentence, he’d have to glance all around the source text to figure out what should come next. “Literally you have your source sentence on the left and your writing on the right, and you’ll be, like, turning your head, left-right, left-right,” he said. “That process is what I expressed as a neural mechanism.”That simplicity seems to me the real tell that this is the real insight. The author does a good job of walking the ready past a long list of distractors and conjuring a sense of a path to an insight, and then, there's the insight - a simple encoding of a simple task: "What is the next word? How do I figure that out? Left-right. Left-right"

item.title: 47. GitHub Actions has added lock files
item.description:
33 points by bengotch on 2026-10-14T14:09:41

GitHub Actions workflow dependency lockfiles are now in public preview for Enterprise Cloud (including data-resin­dency), Team, and Free plans, addressing the risk that tags or branches referenced in workflows can move after review—potentially causing later runs to execute different or malicious code if an action is compromised. Using the `gh actions-lock` GitHub CLI extension, users generate a reviewable `.github/workflows/actions.lock` file that pins actions, their transitive dependencies, and reusable workflows to exact commits; once a workflow is onboarded, Actions runs only the locked commits regardless of tag or branch movement. Onboarding can happen gradually per workflow, and lockfiles can be checked for staleness in CI. A Require lockfile policy, also in preview, lets enterprise, organization, or repository admins mandate lockfiles, while Dependabot automatically regenerates lockfile entries alongside version update PRs. Note that locking pins versions but doesn't vouch for dependency safety, so dependencies should still be reviewed. Setup instructions are in GitHub Docs, with the extension hosted in the public `gh-actions-lock` repo.

item.title: 49. Open source text and image to CAD harness for build123d, OpenSCAD, and smlibpy
item.description:
4 points by bepitulaz on 2026-10-14T22:24:24

MNFT CAD (from "manufacture") is an open-source, Apache-2.0 tool that turns plain-language descriptions into manufacturable 3D parts: you describe a part, a language model writes CAD code, a guarded Python worker runs it via build123d, OpenSCAD, or the alpha SMLib NURBS kernel, and you download STEP, STL, and GLB files plus a rotatable 3D preview in the browser. The project is written in Elixir/OTP and split into four components: `mnft_cad` (the core engine with pluggable engines and storage, no web framework, auth, or database required), `mnft_cad_web` (a Phoenix reference app with a chat UI and anonymous cookie ownership), `mnft_cad_headless` (a headless reference for many concurrent owners and sessions), and `cad_worker` (a small Python CLI with static checks, rlimits, and a hard wall clock around LLM-generated code). It requires Elixir 1.17+, Python 3.11/3.12 with uv, and an LLM API key (BYO-key, multi-provider; poppler is optional for PDF datasheets), and can run via Docker without local Erlang or Python. The embedding guide notes the core never asks who you are — you supply an opaque owner id, storage adapter, engine, and progress handler. The authors caution that the worker's fences protect against mistakes but are not a sandbox, so exposed deployments need kernel-level isolation. The project is built and maintained by Nanas Sound largely with AI coding agents.

item.title: 4. Redesigning source control at Anthropic
item.description:
737 points by Philpax on 2026-10-13T15:49:56

Anthropic built Scion, an in-house centralized version-control system, and migrated its monorepo off git in five months after Claude-driven coding pushed merge volume from ~2,500 code changes per day in May 2026 to over 30,000 per day by September. Git's decentralized design — where every clone holds a complete, offline-capable repository — strained under a main-branch history of nearly 100 GB, a 25+ GB working copy, and ~25 million CI checkouts per day (over 600 PB of naive fetch traffic), forcing the company to run several hundred internal git mirrors plus shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and blob-storage seeds. Scion instead assumes clients are always-online agents and jobs, uses strong client–server asymmetry (the server handles history, blame, commits, merges, and rebases while clients keep only a bounded cache), exposes every source-control query as an API so jobs often need no local repository at all, and is fully horizontally scalable with no materialized repo or packfiles anywhere. Its unit of work is a "changeset" in a write-ahead log that stores only files changed relative to its first parent plus content-addressed pointers to compressed blobs, created server-side with no locking or ref coordination; refs are discouraged except for main and release branches. Additional information — blame, path history, commit-graph skip lists, copy detection, path search — is computed as recursively defined "derived data" that can be added, eagerly or lazily computed, and changed without affecting clients. Servers run as largely independent caches over content-addressed data in Spanner, and the `scn` client fetches recursively by requesting only the specific missing trees and blobs it needs (or the server answers via API), making sparse and virtualized checkouts natural, resumable, and far cheaper than git's packfile protocol. The migration also delivered a code-review surface called Antique, code search, a source-control IAM system, and tooling for landing large volumes of reviewed code; the same period saw automated bisect and revert pipelines become feasible at scale.

item.title: 5. The United Kingdom generates less electricity per person than in the 1970s
item.description:

Roughly 350 million tonnes of plastic waste are produced globally each year, and only about 0.5% of it — around 1.7 million tonnes — ends up in the ocean, according to OECD figures. Most plastic is handled responsibly through secure landfills, recycling, or incineration, while about a quarter is mismanaged or littered; from there, progressively smaller fractions leak into the environment, then rivers and coastlines, and finally the sea. Gapminder's 2020 survey in Sweden, Norway, Finland, Denmark and the UK found nearly nine in ten respondents believed the share was far higher, choosing options of under 36% or 66%. The finding suggests plastic pollution is more tractable than commonly assumed, since effective waste management already exists — the challenge is extending it to all plastic.

Abdulrahman Alfozan, 35, a Saudi national and OpenAI engineer since July 2025, was arrested Friday and charged in federal court with intercepting oral communications after allegedly concealing a recording device in an executive conference room at OpenAI's San Francisco headquarters. OpenAI's technical surveillance countermeasures team found the device on September 30 — plugged into a television's USB port and wrapped in toilet paper, with encrypted contents — and traced its installation to around September 28. Prosecutors say surveillance footage placed Alfozan near the room repeatedly, and that he had used a productivity tool to look up OpenAI's meeting rooms, calendars and leadership locations before the install. On October 5 he allegedly entered the room, looked behind the television, and left a bag containing his wallet, ID and a second similar device unattended elsewhere in the building. OpenAI says it used its own AI models to identify the device and analyze forensic images of its storage, coordinated his firing with the FBI — terminating him the day of his arrest after gradually restricting his access — and has evidence he intended to plant additional recorders in sensitive spaces. The company says it has no indication he accessed model weights, source code or customer data. The U.S. Attorney's office for the Northern District of California is prosecuting, calling the case a national security matter, and FBI Director Kash Patel listed protecting U.S. AI innovation among the bureau's top counterintelligence priorities. item.title: 14. Hittite royal archive found in Turkey
item.description:
368 points by benbreen on 2026-10-13T06:02:51

Archaeologists working at Samuha, the ancient Hittite city in modern-day Sivas, central Turkey, have unearthed 131 cuneiform tablets and fragments this season, adding to 53 found last year and creating the largest Hittite-language archive discovered in the 21st century. Dating to the reign of King Tudhaliya II some 3,400 years ago and written in Hittite and Hurrian, the texts cover an epidemic of fever that killed the king's infant daughter along with the funerary ritual that followed, revealing that the health of royal and elite children was closely monitored by religious leaders who viewed illness as divine will. Another document is a desperate letter from Hittite generals in western Anatolia requesting reinforcements of men, horses and chariots, disclaiming responsibility for any defeat if aid didn't arrive — confirming the king was present at Samuha and underscoring the city's importance as a royal stronghold, later used by Suppiluliuma I as a base for campaigns that expanded the Hittite Empire. The archive also documents Samuha's role as a major religious center dedicated to Sauska, the Hurrian goddess of love and war, and includes a diary-like record of bird diviners' journeys that sheds new light on how Hittite omens were observed and interpreted, alongside correspondence, rituals and prayers that will aid research into Hittite religion, language and scribal culture.

item.title: 18. How to engineer an AI harness for game development
item.description:
146 points by kkukshtel on 2026-10-13T14:14:23

A game developer's write-up of his Indie Rodeo Calgary talk "Your Game Is A Harness," arguing that LLMs struggle with game development not because of inherent limitations but because games are largely opaque to them — unlike web apps, games consist of far more than code, and the training data available is orders of magnitude smaller, so game code the model produces tends to be poor. He recounts his own journey, starting with a ChatGPT-powered moodboarding site (mood.site) built in roughly 20 hours of evenings, which convinced him of LLMs' capability for web stacks while repeated failures on game-specific tasks revealed the gap. After reviewing LLM prompt mechanics — system, assistant, and user prompts, and how every prior message is resubmitted on each turn, causing context accumulation and "context pollution" — he frames the problem as one of context engineering: getting the best information into context with minimal pollution. He introduces "harnesses" (like Claude Code) as sets of expected patterns an agent follows to guide development, noting that while harnesses exist for many domains, none effectively communicate with the game itself, which remains a black box since only the raw code is visible to the model. The solution is to make a game legible to agents — to crack open that black box and make more of it directly addressable. His first concrete recommendation is determinism: fix randomness by establishing a single seeded source of randomness at the start of development and routing all non-deterministic calls through it, making specific states easy to reproduce exactly; adopting this constraint before writing the first line of code avoids a much harder retrofit later. He notes many of these practices improve game development generally, and are simply supercharged by AI.

item.title: 20. Show HN: Parsimony – an open-source benchmark for how much code AI models add
item.description:
66 points by lasu on 2026-10-13T19:50:31

Parsimony is a benchmark that measures how much code AI models add when solving tasks, addressing the fact that existing benchmarks track solve rate and cost but never penalize bloated code. It takes patches already published by benchmarks (SWE-bench Verified), parses the changed Python files without running anything, and counts coding units — statements, calls, comparisons, names and literals — computing net units as added minus removed, so cramming lines earns nothing and deletions are credited. Models are ranked by mean net units added on tasks they solved (lowest first, with a separate figure including failed attempts), while solved counts come from SWE-bench's published results, tests aren't rerun, and an external Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index is shown for context without affecting rank. Self-run experiments on the first 3–10 DeepSWE Python tasks appear faded and unranked, and GPT-5.6 Sol added 0.88× the code in the author's run versus its published run. The site offers interactive charts and a leaderboard (JavaScript required, data on GitHub), acknowledges limits — units capture size rather than readability or design, models that write more code also solve more (Spearman 0.33–0.60), and the mini-SWE-agent itself influences code volume — and lets users download an example JSON file, enter their own benchmark's code-size numbers locally in the browser, and regenerate the same chart and table.

item.title: 22. The Four Colour Theorem: The first time machines mogged mathematicians
item.description:
59 points by list on 2026-10-13T19:17:19

In July 1976, Kenneth Appel and Wolfgang Haken (with programmer John Koch) resolved the century-old Four Color Theorem — that no more than four colors are needed to color any map so no adjacent regions share a color — using roughly 1,200 hours of computer time and 10 billion case checks, launching the era of computer-assisted proof. The reaction among mathematicians was divided: critics like Herbert Wilf, Paul Halmos, Frank Bonsall, Daniel Cohen, and George Spencer-Brown denounced it as unmathematical, an "Oracle," or outright not a proof, with one department head barring the pair from his graduate students for discouraging an elegant human proof; philosopher Thomas Tymoczko later argued an un-surveyable proof isn't a traditional one. Supporters included Bill Tutte (who celebrated in verse), Heinrich Heesch (whose decades of work underpinned the method), and Ted Swart, who countered that computer-assisted proof is "just an extension of pencil and paper" and that humans, unlike machines, tire and slip. Receptivity tracked age — over-40s doubted the computer proof while under-40s doubted 700 pages of hand calculation — and The New York Times initially declined to cover it, later running only an op-ed by Lipman Bers.

Comment Link

Top Comments

  1. That takes me back to an early 1980s incident where I was criticized for an early computer-generated proof. This was when I was building a program verifier at an aerospace company. We had the first SAT solver, the Oppen-Nelson simplifier, and the first constructive theorem prover, the Boyer-Moore prover.[1] I wanted to show that the four axioms of arrays, which the simplifier assumed to be true, were valid in Boyer-Moore theory.Boyer and Moore had warned me of the soundness risks of adding axioms to their prover. So I tried to prove them from basic Boyer-Moore theory, which is close to the Peano axioms. Boyer-Moore theory is LISP-like in form. You start with (ZERO) and (ADD1 X). So two is represented as (ADD1 (ADD1 (ZERO))). It's all lists of tuples at the bottom.Equality is strict. (EQUAL A B) is true only if the representations of both A and B are identical. This creates a problem. An array can be represented as a list of (index, value), but for EQUAL to work, the list has to be ordered by subscript and each subscript unique. So storing into an array is represented as insertion into an ordered list. That generates a lot of special cases.Accessing an array is a linear list search by recursion: (DEFN selecta (A I) (IF (EQUAL (array-elt-subscript A) I) (array-elt-value A) (IF (EQUAL (array-prev A) (empty-array)) (UNDEFINED) (selecta (array-prev A) I)))) That's around line 3276 in [2]. The other definitions of array operations are similarly simple. Then we get to proving the classic four axioms of arrays.Around 3000 lines later, the classic four "axioms" of arrays have been proved. Much grinding through special cases. It's a neat result, but bulky.So I submitted a paper to JACM. Reviewer comments included "I hate to see something this complicated at the foundations of computer science", and just "This is unnecessary." People were really upset by all that case analysis.The theoretical problem was that I didn't have set theory. I could have built up set theory first, before array theory, then used set theory to prove array theory. That probably would have made mathematicians happier. Or not. Set theory is traditionally axiomatic, but it can be built up from constructive Boyer-Moore tuple theory if desired.I didn't argue with the reviewers. I probably could have found a more elegant path to this result, by creating intermediate lemmas, rather than letting the prover grind through the cases on automatic. But I wasn't going for a PhD. I had real work to do at an aerospace company.So, I've been beaten on by the academic community for a bulky machine proof. Today, nobody would be bothered by this approach. It's only a few thousand lines, and a human can follow it. You can be too early.(You can still run this prover today. I converted it to GNU Common LISP a decade ago. It takes about one second on a modern machine to go from the Peano-like axioms to array theory. It took 45 minutes on the VAX 11/780 I was using back in the early 1980s.)[1] https://github.com/John-Nagle/nqthm[2] https://github.com/John-Nagle/pasv/blob/master/src/work/temp...
  2. The problem of the proof was that we knew that FCT was true, but we had no idea why. A good/elegant proof teaches us something new about how that problem is related to other problems. It isn't just about getting a true/false answer to the conjecture.

In robot control, it drives a Boston Dynamics Spot to pick up soda cans and step on a foot-pedal trash bin after practicing in an articulated MuJoCo digital twin; performs zero-shot arm control of a fallen mug and crumpled napkin using a visual coordinate harness, code-as-prolicies primitives, and closed-loop verification; and steers the Gemini Omni video world model in an iterative visual loop to rearrange Scrabble tiles into "ARGON."
